characters: Kofi: a fourteen-year-old Ghanaian JHS 3 boy wearing round glasses, a sky-blue collared school shirt and navy trousers, carrying a graphing calculator and astronomy sketchbook.
Adwoa: his fourteen-year-old classmate, hair styled in neat twists with a headband, wearing the same sky-blue collared school shirt, sharp and inquisitive.
Dr Afia Boateng: a Ghanaian astrophysicist at the planetarium in Accra, wearing a deep indigo blazer over a gold-patterned top.

narrationPlan.voice: Mature, engaging Ghanaian English storyteller (`Kore`) for JHS 2–3.
notes: Use phonetic hints for Kofi, Adwoa, Afia, and Boateng while keeping standard written spellings.

music: Optional subtle cosmic synth pad, off by default.
culturalNotes: Highlights the Ghana Planetarium in Accra and Ghanaian participation in modern astrophysics.
reviewQuestions: Confirm that the distinction between the event horizon and the unresolved interior (quantum gravity) is clear for JHS 2–3.

Kofi (14, round glasses, sky-blue collared shirt, navy trousers) and Adwoa (14, neat twists with headband, sky-blue shirt) looking up at the projected Milky Way galaxy while Dr Afia Boateng (indigo blazer over gold-patterned top) points upward.
pages.narration: Rich, intriguing opening. Emphasise "invisible giant four million times more massive than our Sun".

Dr Afia holding a tabletop orbital model showing Earth on a circular wire track around a glowing yellow Sun sphere, comparing it to a tiny black marble of the same mass.
pages.narration: Emphatic and clear on "A black hole is not a vacuum cleaner" and "Earth would not get sucked in at all".

pages.brief: Planetarium projection showing a massive glowing blue star whose central core is collapsing inward with bright golden light trails (no text), watched by Adwoa and Kofi.
pages.narration: Measured and dramatic. Emphasise "Extreme density" and "collapses under its own weight".

pages.brief: Dr Afia tossing a bright yellow tennis ball gently upward in the planetarium classroom while Kofi and Adwoa follow its path.
pages.narration: Clear, step-by-step explanation of escape velocity.

pages.brief: Glowing visual projection showing golden beams of light curving around a dark sphere; beams outside curve past, while beams crossing the inner boundary spiral in (no words or labels).
pages.narration: Slow and clear on "three hundred thousand kilometres per second" and "event horizon".

pages.brief: Hands-on demonstration table: a dark elastic fabric stretched over a large circular hoop with a heavy brass sphere pressing a deep funnel in the centre; Kofi rolls a glass marble in an orbit around the dip.
pages.narration: Thoughtful and clear. Emphasise how mass curves spacetime.

pages.brief: Adwoa asking a sharp question beside Kofi, while Dr Afia smiles encouragingly in front of the planetarium console.
Planetarium dome showing bright golden elliptical loop tracks of stars orbiting tightly around an unseen central dark point (no text), as Kofi checks his calculator.
pages.narration: Exciting and precise. Pronounce "Sagittarius A-Star" clearly.

pages.brief: Two glowing scientific visualisations on the dome: a fiery orange swirling disk around a dark shadow, and concentric blue ripples radiating from two orbiting black spheres (no text).
pages.narration: Energetic and clear across the second and third lines of evidence.

pages.brief: Kofi and Adwoa looking in awe at the iconic glowing orange ring surrounding a dark central shadow displayed on the main planetarium screen (no text).
pages.narration: Sense of awe and triumph at global radio astronomy teamwork.

pages.brief: Twilight outside the Ghana Planetarium dome in Accra: Kofi holding his sketchbook, Adwoa beside him, and Dr Afia smiling warmly under an indigo sky with bright evening stars.
pages.narration: Honest, inspiring close. Gentle pause before "The end".

teacherGuide.overview: Set at the Ghana Planetarium in Accra, this JHS 2–3 story demystifies black holes using clear physics: debunking the "cosmic vacuum cleaner" myth, explaining escape velocity and the event horizon, presenting four independent lines of observational evidence (stellar orbits around Sagittarius A*, X-ray accretion disks, gravitational waves, and Event Horizon Telescope radio imaging), and highlighting open questions in quantum gravity.
learningGoals: Explain why a black hole is not a cosmic vacuum cleaner and how its gravity at a large distance matches any star of equal mass.
Define escape velocity and explain why light cannot escape from inside the event horizon.
Describe four real astronomical methods used to detect black holes (stellar orbits, accretion-disk X-rays, gravitational waves, and EHT shadow imaging).
Distinguish established relativistic physics from unresolved questions about quantum gravity and the interior of black holes.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "If you throw a stone straight up, why does it come back down? How fast would you have to launch a rocket so it never falls back to Earth?"
Ask what learners have seen about black holes in movies or cartoons, and list their ideas on the board to test against evidence in the story.
whileReading: Pause after page 3 to check understanding of the Sun-replacement thought experiment.
Pause after page 11 to review the four independent lines of evidence that prove black holes exist even though the interior is dark.
afterReading: Revisit the movie myths on the board and have learners correct each one using scientific evidence from the story.
discussion: Why does Earth not get pulled into the Sun right now, and how does that same principle apply to stars orbiting a black hole at a safe distance?
Where does the stretched-cloth model of spacetime work well, and what are its limitations? (See Analogy Note in the Fact-Check Sheet.)
Why did the Event Horizon Telescope need radio dishes spread across multiple continents to photograph M87* and Sagittarius A*?
reflection: How does learning how scientists detect invisible objects in space change the way you think about solving hard problems using indirect clues?

mathsExtension.task: Earth’s escape velocity is about 11 km/s, while the speed of light is about 300,000 km/s. Approximately how many times faster than Earth’s escape velocity is the speed of light? (Round to the nearest thousand.)
Sagittarius A* is about 26,000 light-years away from Earth. How many years does it take for light or radio waves from the centre of the Milky Way to reach our telescopes?
mathsExtension.answer: 26,000 years (because 1 light-year is the distance light travels in 1 year).

support: Use the stretched-cloth and marble demonstration in class so learners can physically see stable orbits far from the central weight versus capture close to the steep centre.
stretch: Research and write a short paragraph on how Ghana’s 32-metre Kuntunse Radio Telescope contributes to Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) networks in Africa.

culturalNotes: The Ghana Planetarium in Accra has inspired thousands of Ghanaian schoolchildren in astronomy and space science.
Kofi, Adwoa, and Afia Boateng are Akan names.
localiseThis: Connect to the Ghana Planetarium (Accra) and the Ghana Radio Astronomy Observatory (Kuntunse).

whatWeKnow: Stellar-mass black holes form from the gravitational collapse of massive stars, and supermassive black holes (millions to billions of solar masses) reside at the centres of most large galaxies, including Sagittarius A* in the Milky Way.
Outside the event horizon, a black hole’s gravitational field obeys Einstein’s general relativity (and approximates Newton’s law of gravitation at large distances).
Astronomers have verified black holes through stellar orbits (2020 Nobel Prize in Physics), gravitational waves (LIGO/Virgo, 2015), X-ray accretion disks, and EHT horizon-scale images (2019, 2022).
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Physicists do not yet have a complete, experimentally verified theory of quantum gravity to describe what replaces the classical "singularity" inside a black hole.
The black hole information paradox, how quantum information is preserved when a black hole slowly evaporates via Hawking radiation, remains an active theoretical question.
Astronomers are still investigating using the James Webb Space Telescope how the earliest supermassive black holes grew so rapidly in the young universe.

investigation.title: Model Gravity and Orbits on a Stretched Cloth
materials: A large plastic basin or bucket (or four students holding the corners of a stretchy cloth taut)
A piece of stretchy T-shirt fabric or lycra cloth
A heavy smooth stone or metal ball
Two or three small glass marbles
steps: Stretch the cloth smoothly and tightly across the top of the basin (or have four learners hold the edges tight and level).
Roll a small marble straight across the flat cloth and observe that it travels in a straight line.
Place the heavy stone in the middle so the cloth curves downward into a funnel, then roll the small marble sideways near the outer edge at a moderate speed so it curves in an orbit around the stone.
Now roll the marble very slowly or aim it closely at the steep central dip and observe how it spirals inward.
investigation.whatToNotice: At a safe distance with enough sideways speed, the marble orbits around the heavy mass without getting "sucked in"; only paths that pass too close or too slowly fall into the steep central well.
investigation.safetyNote: Hold the heavy stone carefully so it does not drop onto toes, and keep small marbles off the floor so nobody slips.

factCheck.claim: Replacing the Sun with a black hole of equal mass would not suck in the Earth; Earth would maintain its orbit.
factCheck.explanation: By Birkhoff’s theorem in general relativity (and Newton’s shell theorem), the external gravitational field at distances much greater than the Schwarzschild radius (r_s ≈ 3 km for 1 solar mass) is identical to that of the Sun.
factCheck.reference: NASA Black Hole Safety & Myths FAQ; Thorne, K. S. (1994), Black Holes and Time Warps.
factCheck.analogyNote: The stretched-cloth analogy helps visualise how mass curves spacetime, but teachers should clarify that real spacetime is 4-dimensional (not a 2D sheet) and balls on a cloth slow down due to friction, whereas space is nearly frictionless.

factCheck.claim: Sagittarius A* (~4 million solar masses) and M87* have been confirmed through stellar orbits, gravitational waves, and Event Horizon Telescope radio interferometry.
factCheck.explanation: Ghez et al. and Genzel et al. tracked star S2 orbiting Sgr A* (2020 Nobel Prize); LIGO detected binary black hole mergers in 2015 (GW150914); the EHT Collaboration published direct shadow images of M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022).
factCheck.reference: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (2019, 2022), Astrophysical Journal Letters; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017 & 2020 Scientific Background.

pronunciation.guidance: Ghanaians often say "uh-KRAH" (stress on the second syllable).

reviewerNotes: Confirm the vowel in the first syllable (oh vs aw).

pronunciation.guidance: "ah-JWAH". The "dw" is the hard part for English engines and is probably not a plain "d" + "w".
